1: Chapter 1: A Visitor on a Rainy Night
It had been raining in Peñaseca for three days. In spring, Lucía Romero’s older sister had left for Madrid, and since then Lucía had run the village’s small apothecary shop alone.
As night fell, she closed the shutters, counted the money she had earned that day, blew out the lamp in one breath, and went upstairs.
She had scarcely lain down when someone knocked hard on the door downstairs. A man’s voice asked, “Is anyone there?”
On the threshold stood a young man soaked to the bone, his left arm wrapped in bloodstained cloth. He said his name was Diego Lobo and that he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
“I need you to treat me,” Lobo said quietly. “I can pay. Will three thousand five hundred reals be enough?”
He took a letter wrapped in wax paper from his jacket. “This letter has to reach the monastery of San Blas before May eighteenth.”
For Lucía, treating that wound was child’s play, but the letter made her uneasy.
Even so, she did not accept his money and only said, “Tomorrow at dawn, I’ll take you to the mountains.”
2: At daybreak, they set off. Lucía carried a basket on her back containing bread, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

Halfway down the slope, they came across old Tomás Gil, who was splitting firewood. He set down his axe and told them in a low voice that three strangers had asked at the entrance to the village about an injured young man the previous evening.
“Go along the trail, Lucía,” Tomás Gil said. “The main road isn’t safe.” Lucía thanked him.
The trail was narrow and slippery. Lucía walked ahead, planting her feet firmly with each step. Lobo followed her in silence.
At noon, the rain stopped, the fog slowly lifted, and the roof of the monastery of San Blas appeared in the distance. A nun, Sister Inés, waited at the door, in charge of receiving visitors.
Sister Inés took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. “The abbess has been waiting for this letter for 2 years.”
Lobo told Lucía, “I owe you my life.” Lucía smiled. “Then, the next time you come, fix the roof of my apothecary for me.” Lobo stayed at the monastery.
At dusk, Lucía descended the mountain alone. By the time she reached home, night had fallen; she lit the lamp and sat behind the counter for a long while.
